title: JPA Relationships
summary: Map Employee and Department relationships, then identify ownership and cascading behavior.

richText: A relationship maps an entity field to another entity or to a collection of entities.
maps many source rows to one target row.
maps one related object on each side.
maps collections on both sides, usually through a join table.
A unidirectional relationship has a Java reference on one side.
A bidirectional relationship has references on both sides.
The owning side supplies the relationship value JPA writes to the database.
For a bidirectional one-to-many relationship, the many-to-one field owns the foreign key.
Its value is the owning Java field name, not a SQL column name.
Both Java references need to agree.
Changing only the inverse collection does not update the owning foreign-key value.

example.title: Map employees to a department
description: The tabs contain all application files for this separate Maven project.
The example requires Java 17 or later, Maven and PostgreSQL with an existing `employee_notes` database.
`database/schema.sql` creates the tables in an empty database before `mvn spring-boot:run`.
Hibernate validates the supplied schema. It does not create the tables.
explanation: A new department must be persisted before an employee refers to it.

richText: A cascade passes a JPA operation from one entity to related entities.
includes all cascade operations, including removal.
removes an owned child when it leaves a one-to-many collection or a one-to-one relationship.
JPA cascades and database foreign-key actions are separate mechanisms.
Removing a shared target with a cascade can remove data other entities still need.
Serializing both sides directly to JSON can follow the same relationship repeatedly.
Response objects can expose only the required values.
